To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
low-frequency ultrasound increases isometric contraction of the smooth muscle of isolated human arteries, but does not affect the relaxation of the smooth muscle.
the application of low-intensity ultrasound to human thoracic arteries resulted in an increase in isometric contractile force of smooth muscles and did not affect the relaxation of the arteries.

low-intensity cavitations induced by low-frequency ultrasound (20 and 32.5 kHz) result in a significant increase in isometric tension in the isolated thoracic artery, which does not depend on exposure number, but does depend on ultrasound frequency and location.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of the effect of cavitation on the isolated human thoracic artery in vitro and the mechanisms underlying this effect.
the study of the influence of ultrasound in the smooth muscle of human thoracic artery.
the effects of ultrasound on human blood vessels and the possibility of their use for the development of new non-invasive methods for the treatment of vascular diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
low-frequency ultrasound has no direct effect on the endothelial-dependent vasodilator function of the human artery.
the ultrasound effect on the human blood vessels is not a direct effect of cavitation, but a result of the interaction between ultrasound waves and the vessel walls.
the low-intensity ultrasound used in the study did not affect the contractile function of smooth muscle and did not improve relaxation of the isolated human thoracic artery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

low-intensity ultrasound is able to modify the contractile state of the smooth muscle in blood vessels and this effect is not dependent on the frequency and number of exposures, but is dependent on the location of the application.
low-intensity ultrasound can be used for the treatment of arterial diseases.

the application of low-frequency ultrasound (20 kHz and/or 32.6kHz) to isolated human arterial samples in vitro results in an increase in the isometric contraction forces and that these forces are not dependent on the frequency and duration of ultrasound, the number of exposures or the time elapsed between the start of ultrasound and the measurement of the force of contraction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ultrasound is capable of inducing a significant increase in the isometric contraction forces of isolated human arteries, which may be a promising method for the treatment of vascular diseases.

ultrasound is capable of inducing a contractile response in the smooth muscle of isolated blood vessels and that this response does not depend on calcium channels or endothelial factors, but does depend on ultrasound frequency and the location of the blood vessels.
ultrasound can be used as an additional therapeutic tool to increase the contractile function of the vascular wall and, consequently, improve blood flow in patients with cardiovascular diseases.
